suggestion.title: npm Preinstall Script Executes Unauthorized Binary
suggestion.rationale: Article directly states 'malicious preinstall binary'—preinstall hooks in package.json run during npm install before any other lifecycle event, a well-known execution vector. No detection rule was generated despite this being core to the attack.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when npm.exe spawns child processes (especially .exe/.bin files) during package installation phases. Flag execution of binaries from node_modules/.bin or npm-cache paths with unknown/unsigned signatures. Correlate with file-write events to sensitive system directories.

suggestion.title: Malicious npm Package Initial Access Indicator
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly identifies 'jscrambler npm package' as compromised. Pipeline failed to extract package name as IOC or flag the supply-chain compromise vector (T1195.003).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install commands against threat-intel feeds of known-malicious packages. Alert on installation of packages with unexpected version bumps, new maintainers, or unusual download timestamps. Flag package.json modifications that introduce preinstall scripts.

suggestion.title: npm Child Process Suspicious Network Behavior
suggestion.rationale: Preinstall binaries typically exfiltrate data or beacon C2. Pipeline should detect outbound connections from npm/node child processes, especially to non-standard ports or external IPs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on network connections initiated by child processes of npm.exe/node.exe to external IPs or domains, especially on non-HTTP ports (443, 8080, 53, custom C2 ranges). Correlate with file exfiltration indicators or process injections.

suggestion.title: Unexpected Binary in node_modules Directory
suggestion.rationale: Preinstall hooks drop binaries to node_modules/.bin, bypassing typical deploy/build controls. Pipeline should flag file creation and execution from this path.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unsigned binaries appearing in node_modules/.bin or node_modules/.bin/ directories. Alert if file hashes don't match known npm packages. Baseline legitimate package binaries; flag novel executables.

suggestion.title: npm Registry Package Metadata Anomaly
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain compromises often show as unexpected version changes or maintainer takeovers. Pipeline should monitor npm registry logs for package ownership/version anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track npm package version history and maintainer changes via npm audit logs or registry snapshots. Alert on rapid version increments, unexpected re-publishes, or version downgrades. Cross-reference with developer alerts if unexpected package updates occur.

suggestion.title: Malicious npm Package Removal/Cleanup Detection
suggestion.rationale: After exploitation, attackers may remove the malicious package or force user updates. Pipeline should detect unexpected package removal or version rollback patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm uninstall or package deletion events in rapid succession after preinstall hook execution. Alert on npm cache purges or selective node_modules deletions that suggest cleanup post-exploitation.

suggestion.title: npm Package Supply Chain Compromise—Known Bad Version Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names jscrambler 8.14.0 as compromised release. Pipeline extracted zero IOCs and no initial-access detections despite title stating 'compromised...npm release.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when npm/yarn installs jscrambler version 8.14.0 or correlate package-lock.json/yarn.lock against threat-intel feeds of compromised versions. Block installation at registry or cache layer. Correlate with subsequent child-process spawning and unsigned binary execution.

suggestion.title: Unsigned Rust Binary Execution from node_modules
suggestion.rationale: Article describes payload that 'drops during install'—npm supply chains commonly stage executables in node_modules or cache. Pipeline missed execution-phase detection entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect process launches where image path resolves to node_modules/*/ or npm cache directories. Rust binaries exhibit distinct PE characteristics (imports, build metadata). Flag unsigned executables in dependency trees, especially those spawned immediately post-install.

suggestion.title: Infostealer Behavioral Collection Indicators
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies threat as 'Rust infostealer'—core capability is harvesting clipboard, screenshots, keystrokes, browser data. Pipeline proposed zero collection-phase detections despite explicit malware family name.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on child processes of Node.js or package-manager processes attempting clipboard reads (GetClipboardData, xclip), screenshot/window capture APIs (BitBlt, PrintWindow, screenshot libs), keystroke hooks (SetWindowsHookEx), or enumerating %APPDATA%, %LOCALAPPDATA%, credential manager stores. Infostealer patterns cluster these within seconds/minutes.

suggestion.title: Malicious postinstall Script Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'drops during install'—postinstall hooks in package.json are standard npm attack vector. Pipeline should have proposed detection on script execution phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor and audit postinstall/install scripts in jscrambler and its dependencies for shell command execution, binary downloads, registry modifications, or obfuscated payloads. Alert on spawning of unexpected child processes (e.g., curl, powershell, cmd.exe) during npm install phase. Analyze script source for suspicious patterns (base64, hex-encoded payloads).

suggestion.title: Exfiltration Traffic from npm-Sourced Processes
suggestion.rationale: Infostealer must transmit stolen data; article establishes malware delivery but pipeline missed command-and-control / exfiltration phase detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on outbound connections initiated by processes under node_modules or spawned by Node.js immediately after installing jscrambler. Flag non-standard ports, high-volume data transfers, TLS renegotiations, or HTTP requests to previously unseen domains. Correlate with infostealer behavioral signatures (e.g., clipboard access → network write within 5 seconds).

suggestion.title: npm Cache and Staging Directory Suspicious File Creation
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'drops...during install'—implies staging in cache or temp. Pipeline missed detection of unexpected binaries written to npm-managed directories during installation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for executable file writes to %AppData%\npm, %AppData%\.npm-global, or system npm cache directories during or immediately after package installations. Flag .exe, .dll, .so, .bin files with missing or suspicious signatures. Correlate creation time with npm install command execution.

suggestion.title: Zimbra RCE via Crafted Email Execution
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states 'crafted emails run malicious code in user sessions'—zero execution-chain detections generated despite this being the core attack.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Zimbra daemon processes (zmmailboxd, zmcontrol, milter) for spawning of cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or interpreter processes. Alert on child processes with parent rooted in MIME-parsing or HTTP handler threads. Correlate with recent email retrieval events.

suggestion.title: Malicious Payload in Email MIME Structure
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'crafted emails' as attack vector—no email content-level detection suggested for embedded scripts or exploit code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect emails with HTML frames, JavaScript event handlers, or base64-encoded scripts in MIME body; prioritize mail to known Zimbra instances. Flag messages with MIME part boundaries containing suspicious Content-Transfer-Encoding or Content-Type values that bypass filtering.

suggestion.title: Zimbra Webmail Session Code Execution
suggestion.rationale: Phrase 'run malicious code in user sessions' indicates execution within authenticated session context—no session-hijacking or privilege-lifting detection generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when processes execute under webmail user context with call stacks rooted in email delivery or rendering engines. Detect unexpected privilege transitions from webmail daemon to system-level operations.

suggestion.title: Post-Compromise Persistence via Email Rules
suggestion.rationale: Successful RCE in user session creates persistence opportunity via forwarding rules—no persistence-layer detection surfaced.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor creation/modification of mail forwarding, delegation, or filter rules immediately following anomalous process activity in Zimbra service. Baseline typical admin rule changes and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: Zimbra Exploitation – Outbound C2 Beaconing
suggestion.rationale: Critical RCE typically followed by C2 callback—no network-level indicators of compromise detection proposed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag unexpected outbound HTTPS/DNS from Zimbra processes to non-whitelisted destinations, especially rapid connections to multiple IPs post-email-delivery. Monitor for DNS exfiltration patterns.

suggestion.title: Zimbra Mailbox Access by Compromised Session
suggestion.rationale: Code execution in user session enables data theft—no mailbox-access anomaly or bulk-export detection generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect rapid or bulk access to mailbox items (attachments, sent items, archive) within user session that was exploited. Alert on unusual export operations or archive downloads outside normal business hours.

suggestion.title: RaaS Affiliate Execution via Living-off-Land Tools
suggestion.rationale: Article keywords flag 'RaaS' model; typical affiliate payload delivery uses psexec, wmic, or schtasks. Article title ('ruthless rise') indicates operational scaling across affiliates.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag parent-child process chains where psexec.exe, wmic.exe, or schtasks.exe spawn cmd.exe or powershell.exe with encoded arguments or scheduled task creation. Correlate timing with failed authentication spikes (credential stuffing) in same window.

suggestion.title: SMB Lateral Movement Post-Initial Access
suggestion.rationale: RaaS operations move laterally before encryption. Keywords mention 'Hospitality Hacks and Retail Reality Checks'—these verticals have flat architecture enabling rapid SMB propagation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Single source initiating SMB sessions to 10+ destinations within 30min, followed by remote process execution (cmd, powershell). Correlate with local credential dumping attempts on originating host.

suggestion.title: Volume Shadow Copy Deletion Before Mass Encryption
suggestion.rationale: Pre-encryption defense evasion step; disables recovery options before encryption loop. Standard RaaS pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect execution of vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all, wmic.exe shadowcopy delete, or Get-WmiObject Win32_ShadowCopy | Remove-WmiObject from non-admin service accounts or immediately post-privilege-escalation.

suggestion.title: Rapid File Writes with Encryption-Signature Extensions
suggestion.rationale: Impact phase: mass file encryption. Hallmark is high-velocity writes to known-file share paths with anomalous extensions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor file writes ≥2000 files/min to common data shares (Documents, Shared, Archive) with single novel extension (.locked, .enc, .gentlemen, .crypt variants). Correlate process with legitimate software baseline (rule out backups, indexing).

suggestion.title: Credential Theft for Double-Extortion Leverage
suggestion.rationale: Modern RaaS combines encryption with data exfiltration. Keywords suggest targeting hospitality/retail—sectors with guest/transaction databases valuable for extortion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag ntdsutil.exe, mimikatz execution, or unusual LSASS access patterns. Monitor for archive creation (.zip, .7z, .tar.gz) in user temp directories immediately after credential dump tools execute.

suggestion.title: Egress of Encrypted Archives to Cloud/Attacker Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Double-extortion exfiltration phase. RaaS affiliates stage data before encryption to enable parallel extortion demand.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate large archive file creation (>500MB) with network egress to high-entropy C2 domains, public cloud storage APIs (AWS S3, Dropbox, Mega, rclone targets), or attacker Tox/onion proxies. Baseline normal egress volumes per user/role.

suggestion.title: Malicious HTML/XSS patterns in SiYuan attribute-view cell JSON
suggestion.rationale: Article states payload breaks out via '' or '">'—these are stored in cell content and never hunted for detection. Pipeline does not look for the XSS payload itself, only downstream command execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search SiYuan attribute-view JSON files (data/storage/av/*.json) for XSS payload indicators: onerror=, onload=, <script>, </textarea> followed by tag-like syntax, embedded javascript: URIs. Correlate JSON modifications with subsequent siyuan.exe process spawning for end-to-end detection. Focus on cells edited by internal users (low false-positive risk if internal user activity is logged).

suggestion.title: SiYuan attribute-view panel opened with stored XSS payload present
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes: 'when the victim opens the block-attribute panel' the XSS fires. This is the critical user-interaction trigger. No detection logic covers the moment an attribute panel is opened and malicious cell data is loaded—only the downstream shell spawning is hunted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate SiYuan process opening/accessing attribute-view JSON files (file open events, mmap patterns on data/storage/av/) with subsequent child process spawning (cmd, PowerShell, etc.) in a tight window. Presence of XSS indicators in the JSON AND child process spawn = exploitation. Reduces false positives vs. shell spawning alone.

suggestion.title: SiYuan database shared/synced to untrusted network or device
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'synced' malicious JSON; if SiYuan supports collaborative or cloud-sync modes, stored payloads can spread. Article also references 'T1080 — Taint Shared Content', implying payloads travel via sync.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor SiYuan process for outbound network connections (HTTP/HTTPS) to non-local or external cloud services while malicious cell data (XSS patterns) exist in the local database. Detect high-frequency attribute-view JSON file reads followed by network uploads, suggesting sync of poisoned data to other devices or servers.

suggestion.title: SiYuan Electron renderer loads/renders untrusted or user-controlled HTML
suggestion.rationale: The core vulnerability is in genAVValueHTML() interpolating cell content without sanitization. The renderer is the execution environment. Detecting unsanitized HTML rendering (or injection of script/onerror tags into DOM) from SiYuan's renderer process would catch the exploitation moment.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor siyuan.exe for suspicious behavior patterns: rapid access to DLLs associated with HTML rendering/WebKit, mmap of large attribute-view JSON files, followed by child process spawning. Alternative: hook renderer logging if SiYuan exposes debug/trace output; look for HTML parse errors or script eval warnings followed by process spawning.

suggestion.title: iCagenda Arbitrary File Upload to iCagenda File Attachment Endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'allows the upload of arbitrary files in the file attachment feature, ultimately resulting in PHP code upload and execution'—core attack vector but zero detection UCs generated for it.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor POST requests to iCagenda file-attachment endpoints with executable extensions (.php, .phtml, .php3, .php5, .php7, .phar) or MIME-type mismatches (e.g., image/* declared but php code in body). Alert on successful 200/201 responses from /components/com_icagenda/upload* or /index.php?option=com_icagenda&task=upload.

suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'PHP code upload and execution' as outcome. No execution-phase detection generated despite this being the post-compromise impact.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag PHP interpreter spawning (php.exe, php-cgi.exe, httpd children executing PHP) from web-accessible upload directories matching iCagenda paths. Correlate with prior file-upload events to chain initial compromise to code execution.

suggestion.rationale: CISA KEV entry means active, in-the-wild exploitation—IDS/IPS and WAF should detect known PoC patterns and reconnaissance signatures targeting this CVE.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP requests matching iCagenda file upload endpoint paths (e.g., /index.php with file attachment parameters). Alert on Shodan/Censys scanning patterns probing for iCagenda version disclosure. Cross-reference threat feeds for CVE-2026-48939 PoC exploit payloads and attacker user-agents.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Command Execution in iCagenda Context
suggestion.rationale: After PHP upload, attacker can execute arbitrary commands. Article describes leading to code execution without further context—hunt for command-line activity spawned from the web application.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for process creation by the web server process (apache, nginx, php-fpm) launching bash, sh, or cmd.exe. Correlate with timestamps following successful PHP file uploads. Flag unusual process arguments (wget, curl, nc, base64-encoded commands).

suggestion.title: iCagenda Installation Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Attackers probe for vulnerable iCagenda instances before exploitation. Article emphasizes 'actively exploited'—precursor recon patterns should be detected before actual exploit attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for multiple requests probing iCagenda version endpoints (/administrator, common component paths, error pages disclosing version). Flag multiple enumeration requests from the same source over short time windows without legitimate user session context.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-48939 Asset Exposure Hunt
suggestion.rationale: CISA KEV article explicitly states active exploitation in the wild; federal patch due 2026-07-13. Article text: 'iCagenda contains an unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability.' Must locate all exposed instances before exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search internal and external vulnerability scanners for hosts running iCagenda version < [patched version]. Cross-reference with network exposure data (internet-facing on ports 80/443). Correlate scanner banner-grab data or HTTP response headers containing 'iCagenda' signature.

suggestion.title: PHP File Upload to iCagenda Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'allows the upload of arbitrary files in the file attachment feature, ultimately resulting in PHP code upload and execution.' Direct exploitation requires uploading .php/.phtml files; monitor for this pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor POST/PUT requests to iCagenda upload endpoints (typical paths: /attachments, /media, /upload) with Content-Disposition or filename parameters containing .php, .phtml, .php3, .php4, .php5, .pht, .phps extensions. Alert on 200/201 responses followed by GET requests to newly created files.

suggestion.title: Web Process Anomalous Child Process Execution
suggestion.rationale: After PHP upload executes, OS-level command execution occurs. Article: 'PHP code upload and execution' implies arbitrary code execution context. Monitor web service accounts spawning unexpected processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect php.exe, apache.exe, or w3wp.exe processes spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, wget, or nc with high confidence. Baseline: PHP should invoke known-good libraries only; cmd/powershell invocation is anomalous. Filter on iCagenda directory context if available.

suggestion.title: iCagenda Attachment Directory File Integrity Monitoring
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'file attachment feature' – new/modified files in attachment storage are direct evidence of upload exploitation. FIM can trigger before process execution is observed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor iCagenda attachment directories for creation or modification of files with dangerous extensions (.php, .jsp, .asp, .phtml, .exe, .dll, .sh, .pl) within 5 minutes of failed/anomalous HTTP requests. Alert on timestamp clustering (multiple uploads in short window).

suggestion.title: iCagenda Upload Endpoint HTTP 5xx or Repeated 413 Errors
suggestion.rationale: Failed exploitation attempts will trigger errors. Article describes 'arbitrary files' upload; payload size or type rejection logs indicate attack traffic even if blocked.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate HTTP 413 (Payload Too Large), 400 (Bad Request), 403 (Forbidden), or 500 errors on iCagenda upload endpoints with attacker IP geolocation or known-threat-actor ASNs. Cluster by source IP and endpoint; multiple failures from same source in 10-minute window indicate reconnaissance or brute-force upload attempts.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-48939 IOC: Vulnerability Scanner Detection Match
suggestion.rationale: Primary IOC is the CVE itself. Article: 'CVE-2026-48939' is the canonical identifier for this vulnerability; patch due 2026-07-13 drives urgent scanning.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt vulnerability scanner output for CVE-2026-48939 matches. Cross-reference asset name/IP with iCagenda product registry. Suppress false negatives (patched hosts confirming patch date; unpatched hosts triggering incident response). Correlate with external SHODAN/Censys snapshots to confirm internet exposure.

suggestion.title: iCagenda Suspicious File Upload Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability that allows the upload of arbitrary files in the file attachment feature.' Pipeline generated zero file-upload detections despite this being the primary attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP POST requests to iCagenda file attachment endpoints (typically /upload, /attachment, /media). Flag requests uploading files with executable extensions (.php, .phtml, .php3, .php4, .php5, .phar, .inc) or polyglot payloads (double extensions like .php.jpg). Alert on HTTP 200/201 responses indicating successful upload.

suggestion.title: PHP Code Execution Following iCagenda Upload
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'PHP code upload and execution' as the exploitation outcome. Pipeline missed the execution phase entirely—no use cases for detecting post-upload code execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate suspicious file uploads to iCagenda with child process spawning from web server workers (apache2, nginx, php-fpm, php-cgi). Flag execution of shell interpreters or script engines launched by httpd UID/GID within seconds of upload activity. Monitor for unusual process arguments indicating command execution via PHP (exec(), system(), shell_exec()).

suggestion.title: iCagenda Web Application Error Spikes
suggestion.rationale: Exploitation attempts typically leave error traces in application logs. Article describes a feature-level vulnerability; failed uploads may generate diagnostic errors before successful exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor iCagenda application error logs and web server error logs for sudden spikes in HTTP 400/413/415/500 responses on upload endpoints. Flag specific error patterns related to file validation bypass, MIME-type mismatches, or permission errors. Baseline normal upload traffic and alert on 10x deviation within 5-minute windows.

suggestion.title: Suspicious PHP File Creation in Web-Accessible Directories
suggestion.rationale: Successful exploitation results in 'PHP code upload.' Pipeline missed detection for file-system artifacts created by the attack. Web-shell persistence requires detecting new .php files in upload/attachment directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for new .php, .phtml, .php3, .php4, .php5 file creation in iCagenda upload directories (/uploads, /attachments, /media, /files) by httpd/www-data/nginx processes or via non-user accounts. Flag files with creation time matching HTTP upload requests. Alert on files containing web-shell signatures (eval, system, exec, passthru keywords).

suggestion.title: iCagenda CVE-2026-48939 Scanner Queries
suggestion.rationale: Article is from CISA KEV—federal mandate is to scan infrastructure for CVE-2026-48939. Pipeline extracted zero IOCs. Vulnerability scanner correlation is the baseline detection for any known-exploited vulnerability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query vulnerability management platform for hosts flagged as vulnerable to CVE-2026-48939 (iCagenda). Cross-reference against external-facing asset inventory and patch management CMDB to identify instances with patch lag >7 days (federal due date 2026-07-13). Escalate any unpatched exposures directly to remediation queue.

suggestion.title: iCagenda Polyglot/Null-Byte File Extension Bypass Uploads
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'dangerous type vulnerability'—common evasion is double extension (.php.jpg) or null-byte injection (.php%00.jpg). Pipeline generated zero payloads/bypass detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor iCagenda upload requests for file names containing null bytes, double extensions, or case variations (.PhP, .pHp). Inspect HTTP multipart form data Content-Disposition filename parameter for polyglot patterns. Flag requests with filename like 'shell.php.jpg', 'shell.jpg.php', 'shell.php%00.jpg', or 'shell.php;.jpg'.

suggestion.title: File Upload to iCagenda with Dangerous Extension
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type' and 'arbitrary files in the file attachment feature'—pipeline missed detection for .php, .phtml, .php3, .php4, .php5, .phar uploads to iCagenda endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor POST/PUT to iCagenda file attachment endpoints for dangerous extensions. Flag requests where filename ends in .php* or .phar but Content-Type claims innocent type (image/jpeg). Look for multipart/form-data uploads with file parameter mismatch.

suggestion.title: PHP Code Execution from Web Upload Directory
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'PHP code upload and execution'—pipeline omitted detection for PHP interpreter spawning from web root after upload event, indicating successful exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate file creation in web-accessible upload directories with PHP process execution (php.exe, php-cgi) sourcing that file within 0–5 minutes. Alert on unexpected parent processes (w3wp.exe, httpd, nginx) spawning PHP interpreters reading from recent uploads.

suggestion.title: Web Shell Artifact Detection in iCagenda Upload Directories
suggestion.rationale: Article implies persistent execution via uploaded PHP—pipeline missed hunt for web shell indicators (base64_decode, eval, $_GET, $_POST, passthru) in upload directory post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan iCagenda upload directory for PHP files with creation timestamps post-2026-07-10, obfuscated variable names ($a, $_, base64_), and known webshell signatures. Flag files with <200 bytes of recognizable source or large base64 blocks.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-48939 Vulnerability Scanner Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies CVE-2026-48939 as exploit IOC—pipeline failed to create baseline hunt: vulnerability scanner flagging iCagenda as unpatched for this CVE.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any asset inventory entry identifying iCagenda product with CVE-2026-48939 unpatched status. Cross-reference with web proxy logs for iCagenda-specific signatures or known admin paths from external sources.

suggestion.title: iCagenda Endpoint Probing and Upload Bypass Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article notes 'unrestricted upload'—attackers probe endpoints before exploit. Pipeline missed detection for failed uploads (403, 405, 413) followed by successful upload, indicating bypass enumeration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor iCagenda upload endpoints for sequences of failed HTTP responses (405 Method Not Allowed, 413 Payload Too Large, 403 Forbidden) followed by success (200/201). Flag repeated requests with variant file extensions (.php, .php5, .phtml, .phar) in same session.

suggestion.title: iCagenda Arbitrary File Upload to Web Directory
suggestion.rationale: Article core: 'allows the upload of arbitrary files in the file attachment feature' — this is the initial exploitation vector and must be detected at the upload boundary.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor POST requests to iCagenda file-upload endpoints (*/uploads/*, */attachments/*, */media/*) for suspicious file extensions (.php, .phtml, .php3, .phar) or MIME type mismatches (e.g., application/x-php uploaded as image/jpeg).

suggestion.title: PHP Webshell Creation via iCagenda Upload
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'PHP code upload and execution' — detection must capture the file-system write of executable PHP to web-accessible paths.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on creation of .php, .php3, .phtml files in document root or iCagenda subdirectories (esp. */uploads/*, */cache/*) within seconds of POST requests to upload endpoints.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-48939 Exploitation Attempt Pattern
suggestion.rationale: CISA KEV entries are in-the-wild exploitation; pattern-based detection on known exploit attempts or vulnerable endpoint signatures is standard for actively-exploited vulns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline iCagenda file-attachment request patterns and flag requests matching known exploitation signatures (e.g., multipart uploads with executable MIME types, POST payloads from public exploit PoCs).

suggestion.title: Post-Upload PHP Execution via HTTP GET
suggestion.rationale: After webshell upload, attacker invokes it via GET; detecting the HTTP request + subsequent child-process spawn closes the execution detection loop.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate HTTP GET requests to recently-uploaded .php files (within last 5 min) with child-process spawning (bash, curl, powershell) by the web server process (httpd, apache2, php-fpm).

suggestion.title: iCagenda Vulnerable Asset Inventory
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Federal patch due: 2026-07-13' — asset detection and patch-status validation must run immediately for actively-exploited vulns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query asset inventory and banner-grab iCagenda instances to confirm version >= [patched]; flag unpatched instances for immediate remediation and enhanced monitoring.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Installation – Miasma Variant Hashes
suggestion.rationale: Article headline indicates npm packages were compromised; pipeline extracted zero IOCs. Should detect installation of AsyncAPI packages with known-malicious file hashes or version identifiers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install/package.json resolution for AsyncAPI package versions tagged as compromised. Correlate against known Miasma variant SHA256 hashes from advisory. Alert if package-lock.json or node_modules contains flagged hashes.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Compromise – Malicious npm Registry Request Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article states AsyncAPI packages were compromised; implies attackers modified packages on npm registry. Detect unusual registry queries or package fetch behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify npm registry requests to atypical mirrors, or package.json references to alternative registries (e.g., non-official npm.js URLs). Correlate package names against AsyncAPI CVE/advisory list.

suggestion.title: Miasma Malware Execution – Dropper / Post-Install Script Behavior
suggestion.rationale: Miasma variant introduced via npm package; likely executes via install scripts (postinstall hooks). Article likely describes execution payload but not extracted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm install/postinstall scripts spawning PowerShell, bash, or native binaries with suspicious arguments (e.g., curl/wget to C2, file enumeration, registry access). Flag unusual child processes from node.exe.

suggestion.title: Miasma C2 Beaconing – Exfiltration to Known Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Malware family name 'Miasma' implies specific TTPs; article likely identifies C2 domains/IPs not extracted by pipeline.

suggestion.title: Sanctioned VPN Service C&C Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'VPN Service' involvement in ransomware support operations. Pipeline extracted no C&C or network-anonymization detections. Phrase: 'Sanctions First VPN Service...Over Ransomware Support'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound connections to known-sanctioned VPN provider domains or ASNs with ransomware-typical patterns (sustained connection during high disk I/O, correlation with file-read loops). Flag VPN tunnel establishment followed by bulk network discovery.

suggestion.title: Ransom Note Creation & Bulk File Encryption
suggestion.rationale: Ransomware attacks inherently produce ransom notes and encrypted file masses. Article emphasizes ransomware-support infrastructure; pipeline missed both the impact phase and pre-impact staging. Phrase: 'Ransomware Support'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect mass file creation of .txt or .html ransom notes alongside rapid file extension changes (legitimate-to-.ransomware-ext) in user profile or shared drives. Alert on >10% of drive encrypted in <1 hour; correlate with VSS deletion and backup-mount enumeration.

suggestion.title: Threat Actor Network Discovery Pre-Encryption
suggestion.rationale: Ransomware-as-a-service operations require network reconnaissance before encryption. Pipeline omitted discovery-phase detections. Article context implies multi-stage attack for maximizing ransom.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect parent-child chains: net.exe/quser/systeminfo followed by file-share enumeration (dir \\*\c$, net view \\*). Flag Get-ChildItem recursion on network paths, concurrent SMB 445 handshakes to multiple subnets, and WMI queries (Win32_Share, Win32_LogicalDisk).

suggestion.title: Sanctioned Entity Infrastructure Access Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Article is about sanctions enforcement; pipeline should flag infrastructure IOCs (domains, ASNs, payment wallets) associated with the named VPN and cryptor sellers. No IOCs extracted at all.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain a sanctioned-provider blocklist (VPN domains, cryptor-seller hosting, payment infrastructure) and alert on any direct connection attempts, DNS queries, or HTTP requests. Cross-reference with known ransomware-affiliate infrastructure for early warning.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Installation from Untrusted Registry
suggestion.rationale: Article states packages were 'disguised as student proxies'—malicious npm packages installed via dependency resolution. Article phrase: '148 npm Packages Disguised as Student Proxies'. Pipeline missed detection for supply-chain compromise entry point.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install / yarn / pnpm execution for packages with malicious indicators: names mimicking proxy tools, zero/minimal download history, registry timestamps inconsistent with user history. Alert on suspicious package manifests referencing external scripts or postinstall hooks reaching unknown C2.

suggestion.title: NodeJS Process Establishing Unexpected Outbound Connections
suggestion.rationale: DDoS botnet requires C2 communication. Article: 'Turned Browsers Into a DDoS Botnet' implies command-and-control callbacks from browser/node contexts. Pipeline did not model C2 detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline of legitimate node_modules network egress. Alert on node.exe, node processes spawned by browsers, or script engines opening connections to non-standard ports, international IPs (especially if not correlating to CDN), or repeated re-connection attempts characteristic of botnet heartbeats.

suggestion.title: Browser JavaScript Injection and Malicious Script Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article describes browser transformation into DDoS bot. Malicious code injected via npm→browser. Article phrase: 'Turned Browsers Into a DDoS Botnet'. Pipeline missed behavioral signatures of JavaScript execution and injection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor browser processes (Edge, Chrome, Firefox) for suspicious child process spawning, WebSocket or XMLHttpRequest to attacker C2, or in-memory injection patterns. Cross-reference with npm package installation timeline to correlate postinstall hooks with browser compromise timing.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Outbound HTTP/S Traffic from Browser DDoS Bot
suggestion.rationale: Compromised browsers executing DDoS on external targets. Article: 'Turned Browsers Into a DDoS Botnet'. Pipeline did not suggest impact/exfiltration detection (traffic volume, request patterns).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect anomalous traffic volume or rate from single browser instances: sustained > 1000 req/s, target-agnostic flooding patterns, or Request headers identical across floods (fingerprint of script-driven botnet vs. user traffic). suggestion.title: npm Registry or Package Repository Tampering Detection
suggestion.rationale: 148 packages uploaded or modified by attacker. Article: 'npm Packages Disguised as Student Proxies' implies account compromise or registry injection. Pipeline missed registry-layer detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm/yarn package repository access logs for: new package uploads by inactive or suspicious accounts, version bumps with changed package size / hash not matching source repo, metadata injection (homepage, repository URLs pointing to attacker infrastructure), or rapid publish-unpublish cycles indicative of testing malicious artifacts.

suggestion.title: Compromised npm Account Behavioral Anomalies
suggestion.rationale: Attack likely required compromised maintainer accounts or new attacker-owned accounts with rapid org/team membership escalation. Pipeline did not model auth/account layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on npm account logins from new geographic regions, new API tokens generated and immediately used for package publish, bulk package publishing by low-reputation or newly-created accounts, or accounts suddenly shifting from consumer (install) to publisher (release) profile.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Salesforce API Token Creation or Unauthorized API Access
suggestion.rationale: ShinyHunters campaigns consistently pivot through API tokens to maintain persistence and escalate access within SaaS targets. Article describes 'three Salesforce attack paths'—API abuse is standard for Salesforce-focused threat actors. Look for: 'Three Salesforce Attack Paths' implies API-centric exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect API token creation events outside normal maintenance windows, API calls from IPs/geolocations inconsistent with user baseline, and token usage spikes within minutes of creation. Flag OAuth tokens generated by service accounts during non-business hours or with overly permissive scopes (data:read, data:write on sensitive objects).

suggestion.title: Salesforce Mass Data Export or Unusual SOQL Query Volume
suggestion.rationale: ShinyHunters operates as a data-theft-for-hire group; article title highlights year-long campaign implying sustained exfiltration. Salesforce breaches typically manifest as bulk queries or exports of customer/opportunity records.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on SOQL queries returning >10k rows in single session, data exports initiated by non-Admin accounts, or API calls to /services/data/v**/query or bulk API endpoints returning unexpectedly large result sets. Correlate with off-hours access patterns.

suggestion.title: Phishing or Credential Harvest Targeting Salesforce Admins/Users
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'year of ShinyHunters Activity'—initial access for Salesforce compromises typically relies on phishing or credential reuse. No IOCs or phishing indicators extracted despite critical severity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for emails containing Salesforce-lookalike domains, requests for MFA codes or session tokens, and credential submission to non-Salesforce endpoints. Cross-correlate with Salesforce login failures followed by successful logins from new IP/device within hours.

suggestion.title: MFA Bypass or Session Hijacking via Stolen Cookies/Tokens
suggestion.rationale: Salesforce-targeting campaigns routinely bypass MFA through token theft or session fixation. Article states 'three attack paths'—MFA evasion likely comprises at least one pathway for sustained access.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Salesforce logins with MFA disabled or bypassed, session_id reuse across non-adjacent IPs, or successful logins immediately after failed MFA attempts. Flag browser/device fingerprint changes within same session.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement Within Salesforce: Privilege Escalation to Admin or Custom Roles
suggestion.rationale: Once inside Salesforce, threat actors escalate to admin or high-privilege roles to access sensitive data and modify audit logs. Year-long campaign indicates sustained lateral movement within the platform.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on role assignment changes (especially to Admin or custom high-privilege roles) from non-HRIS automation accounts, permission set group additions by unexpected users, and sharing rule modifications enabling org-wide access to sensitive objects.

suggestion.title: Salesforce Audit Log Deletion or Modification Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Sophisticated actors disable or delete audit logs to cover tracks. Article describes 'year of activity'—any campaign lasting >3 months without log tampering is rare. No defensive indicators extracted by pipeline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for login history record deletions, audit trail export or archival to unexpected destinations, disable of audit logging features (if permissions allow), or gaps in audit timestamps suggesting tampering. Cross-check against immutable cloud logging backups.

suggestion.title: Kimai: Successful Authentication Without Credential Entry
suggestion.rationale: Article states attacker can 'forge HMAC-signed cookies' and achieve 'account takeover.' This is the core exploitation path—detect authentication events (session creation, privilege escalation actions) that occur without corresponding password entry or login process. Cite: 'forge HMAC-signed cookies'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag successful Kimai authentication to admin or privileged accounts when the session bearer token (Symfony PHPSESSID or equivalent) appears in access logs without a preceding login event in the Kimai auth log or without password submission captured in web proxy.

suggestion.title: Kimai: Deployment with Unmodified Default APP_SECRET
suggestion.rationale: Article warns 'Docker entrypoint does not override or validate' the default secret value. Detect containers deployed with default configuration. Cite: 'Docker image ships with APP_SECRET=change_this_to_something_unique... does not override'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan Kimai container image deployments for missing or unset APP_SECRET environment variable override. Compare deployment manifests, container runtime config, and image metadata against hardened baselines that require explicit APP_SECRET configuration.

suggestion.title: Kimai: Suspicious Web Session Bulk Operations Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Once attacker forges cookie and gains 'account takeover,' they will perform lateral movement or data exfiltration. Monitor for bulk timesheet modifications, user creation, or configuration changes tied to hijacked sessions. Cite: 'account takeover' and Kimai's time-tracking purpose.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate session IDs with bulk write operations (mass timesheet edits, user/project creation, rate changes). Flag sessions showing off-hours or impossible-travel bulk modifications inconsistent with the legitimate account holder's behavior.

suggestion.title: Kimai: Impossible Travel Detection on Authentication Sessions
suggestion.rationale: Forged cookies can originate from attacker-controlled infrastructure. Detect session IPs and user-agents that violate geographic/temporal plausibility. Cite: 'unauthenticated attacker' forging cookies from arbitrary network locations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track Kimai session IPs, user-agents, and source locations per account. Flag sessions from IPs thousands of kilometers apart within seconds, or sessions from countries/ASNs never accessed by the account previously.

suggestion.title: Kimai: HTTP Cookie Header Anomalies (Known-Secret Signatures)
suggestion.rationale: If Kimai logs or proxies capture full cookie headers, HMAC-forged cookies may exhibit patterns (timestamps, signature structure) consistent with the known APP_SECRET. Cite: 'forge HMAC-signed cookies' using 'publicly-known Symfony kernel.secret'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Collect and parse Symfony session cookies (if readable in logs). Correlate cookie HMAC signatures against the known default APP_SECRET hash to identify forged cookies in web traffic.

suggestion.title: Kimai: Docker Image Scanning for Hardcoded Default Secrets
suggestion.rationale: Article's root cause is default secret in the official Docker image. Proactive detection should scan images pre-deployment. Cite: 'official Kimai Docker image ships with APP_SECRET=change_this_to_something_unique'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan Kimai container images (registry names, tags matching Kimai) for hardcoded environment variables, .env files, or config artifacts containing the string 'change_this_to_something_unique' or Kimai's documented default secrets.

suggestion.title: TOTP Brute-Force via Unauthenticated 2FA Endpoint (UC_10_1 corrected)
suggestion.rationale: Article states endpoint 'accepts unauthenticated POST containing only fsNick and fsTwoFactorCode' with TOTP that is 'brute-forceable'; pipeline generated no detections for the core exploit. suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for POST requests to /login?action=two-factor-validation from same source with 5+ distinct fsTwoFactorCode values in <300 seconds. Flag if request lacks prior session password authentication. Look for 401/403→200 response cascade indicating brute-force success. Correlate with immediate downstream authentication or sensitive operations.

suggestion.title: Session Creation Without Password Verification
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states handler 'does not verify the password' yet 'issues full fsNick + fsLogkey session cookie pair'; anomalous authentication flow bypass should be detected at credential creation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on session cookie issuance (fsLogkey created) from 2FA endpoint (/login?action=two-factor-validation) when no password-authentication event (hash check, password field submission, or MFA prompt initiation) appears in same session within prior 5 minutes. Indicates bypass of normal login flow.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Account Abuse After 2FA Bypass
suggestion.rationale: Successful exploitation grants full account access; pipeline should include hunt for behavioral divergence from baseline following suspicious 2FA activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate anomalous 2FA session creation with subsequent atypical user activity: invoking admin functions, exporting sensitive data, creating API tokens, modifying account settings, accessing resources outside baseline geography/time-of-day. Flag if baseline profile or geographic travel is impossible.

suggestion.title: Reconnaissance: Enumeration of FacturaScripts /login Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article describes vulnerability in public /login endpoint; attackers must first discover FacturaScripts instances. Pipeline provided no reconnaissance-phase detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP 200/302 responses to /login endpoints from script-like user-agents (curl, Python-requests, Nmap, etc.) with rapid sequential probing. Flag sources explicitly querying /login?action=two-factor-validation, indicating targeted reconnaissance for this CVE endpoint.

suggestion.title: Cisco IOS Web Interface CSRF Exploitation via /level/15/exec/ URIs
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names exploit URIs: '/level/15/exec/-' and '/level/15/exec/-/configure/http'. States these enable 'arbitrary commands' execution. Pipeline extracted zero use cases despite clear HTTP-based attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP GET/POST requests to Cisco IOS web interface on ports 80, 443, or device management ports targeting /level/15/exec/* paths. Correlate with Cisco device configuration/command logs for unexpected execution within seconds of suspicious HTTP requests.

suggestion.title: Cisco IOS Remote Arbitrary Command Execution Post-CSRF
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability 'allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via (1) show privilege (2) alias exec commands'. No execution-phase detection generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Cisco device logs for privilege-level-15 command execution without corresponding SSH/console login sessions. Flag atypical source IPs issuing commands via web interface (check syslog for HTTP-originated sessions).
